name: Consequentialism
statement: An action is right or wrong solely according to its consequences; the best outcome makes the right act.
meaning: Consequentialism is a class of normative ethical theories holding that the morality of an action, its rightness or wrongness, depends only on its consequences or outcomes, so that the right action is the one that produces the best overall outcome. It is a teleological ethics, focused on the ends or goals an action brings about, and its rough popular gloss is that the ends justify the means. Consequentialism stands opposed to deontology, which grounds rightness in duties, rules, or rights independent of outcomes, and it differs from virtue ethics, which centers on character rather than on the results of particular acts. The most famous form of consequentialism is utilitarianism, associated with Jeremy Bentham and John Stuart Mill, which holds that the right act is the one that maximizes overall happiness or well-being, often summarized as the greatest good for the greatest number. Other forms include ethical egoism, which maximizes the good for oneself, and rule consequentialism, which judges acts by rules whose general adoption best maximizes the good. Consequentialists must specify what counts as a good outcome, whether pleasure, well-being, preference-satisfaction, or something else, and whose consequences count. Consequentialism is one of the three major approaches in normative ethics.
mechanism: Consequentialism evaluates actions by looking forward to their results rather than backward to duties or inward to character. To determine whether an action is right, the consequentialist asks what its consequences would be and compares them with the consequences of the available alternatives; the right action is the one whose outcome is best. This requires a theory of the good, an account of what makes an outcome better or worse, and different consequentialists offer different answers: hedonists count pleasure and the absence of pain, welfarists count well-being, preference theorists count the satisfaction of preferences, and pluralists count several goods. It also requires a view of whose good counts and how it is aggregated; classical utilitarianism is agent-neutral and impartial, counting everyone's good equally, while ethical egoism counts only the agent's own good. A key division is between act consequentialism, which judges each individual act directly by its consequences, and rule consequentialism, which judges acts by whether they conform to rules whose general acceptance would produce the best consequences, a move meant to soften some objections. Because consequences unfold over time and across many people, applying the theory requires predicting outcomes, which is often difficult. The unifying core is that nothing about an act other than its consequences ultimately determines whether it is right.

examples.text: For a consequentialist, the right action is simply the one that produces the best overall consequences among the alternatives.
The most famous consequentialist theory, utilitarianism, holds that the right act maximizes overall happiness or well-being.
Act consequentialism judges each act by its consequences, while rule consequentialism judges acts by the best rules to adopt.

variants.name: Act versus rule consequentialism
variants.text: Judging each act directly by its consequences, versus judging acts by rules whose general adoption best maximizes the good.

variants.name: Theories of the good
variants.text: The differing accounts of what counts as a good outcome, from pleasure to well-being to preference-satisfaction.

whyItMatters: Consequentialism is one of the three major approaches in normative ethics and among the most influential frameworks for thinking about right and wrong. Its central idea, that the morality of an action depends on the goodness of its outcomes, is intuitive and powerful, and it underlies a vast amount of practical moral and political reasoning: cost-benefit analysis, welfare economics, public policy, and utilitarian arguments in bioethics and animal welfare all rest on broadly consequentialist thinking about maximizing good outcomes. By making the results of actions the measure of their rightness, consequentialism offers a clear, impartial, and in principle calculable standard, and it forces attention to the actual effects of our choices on the well-being of everyone affected. As the leading rival to deontology and virtue ethics, it defines much of the debate in moral philosophy, and objections to it, that it can justify sacrificing individuals for the greater good, that it is too demanding, or that it neglects rights and integrity, have themselves shaped ethical theory. Whether embraced or resisted, consequentialism provides an indispensable lens for moral analysis.

working.text: evaluate an action by the consequences it would produce, not by duties or character.
weigh the outcome of each available action against a theory of what makes outcomes good.
identify the right action as the one whose consequences are best overall.

limits: Consequentialism faces powerful objections that have shaped ethical theory. Because it makes outcomes the sole measure of rightness, it can seem to justify intuitively monstrous acts when they produce the best consequences, as in the transplant case, where killing one healthy person to harvest organs and save five appears to maximize good, or in punishing an innocent to prevent a riot; critics argue this shows it neglects rights and justice. It is also charged with being excessively demanding, since it may require constant self-sacrifice for marginal gains to others, and with ignoring the distribution and fairness of outcomes and the separateness of persons. Bernard Williams's integrity objection holds that by focusing only on consequences and holding agents responsible for all the good they fail to produce, consequentialism can alienate people from their own projects and commitments. Predicting and comparing all the consequences of an action is also often practically impossible.
misreadings: Consequentialism does not say any means are acceptable if the goal is good in a loose sense; it says the rightness of an act depends on its actual overall consequences, which is why critics press cases where good outcomes seem to require terrible acts. It is not a single theory but a family, including act and rule versions and different theories of the good. And it is not obviously correct, since objections about rights, demandingness, and integrity are serious, so treating consequentialism as endorsing any ruthless means, as one uniform view, or as beyond challenge, misreads a major but contested approach to ethics.
origin: A class of normative ethical theories, one of the three major approaches in ethics, holding that the morality of an action depends only on its consequences; its most famous form is utilitarianism.

Consequentialism, Encyclopaedia Britannica. — the doctrine that actions are judged right or wrong by their consequences, and utilitarianism as its simplest form.
